People of means don't fly budget airlines - they want premium services and are willing to pay for them. That leaves airlines like Spirit in a constant budget hole because their target audience is SO price-elastic - they generally only care about the bottom line cost to get from point A to point B - which results in a constrained revenue stream right from the beginning. This kind of revenue constraint makes a 'budget anything' extremely vulnerable to any operating cost variables that don't work in its favor. The argument Mr. Kahan seems to be making is, 'why couldn't we offer premium perks like the stronger competitors?' See above.

But once you decide to depart from the old system (rigid rules but a lot of quiet cheating), you had better forget about doing the job piecemeal or gradually:  build a completely new model, or don't other. It provides a victim of gun violence funds to cover medical and counseling expenses. This part of insurance only works if the gun and owner can be identified after the loss is incurred. Insurance also provides incentives for owners to get safety training, use proper storage and security.  But most importantly widespread use of insurance will provide the future with very detailed actuarial data on every aspect of gun ownership, use and the losses from gun use.  This feature may be one reason gun insurance is not being considered. China didn’t simply “steal American technology,” as the common narrative sometimes suggests. It's an easy narrative for politicians and China hawks in DC. China is an easy target these days, just as Soviet during the Cold War, Iran in the Post-9/11, Japan in the 1980s. Technology transfer between China and the US has involved many different channels, including legitimate trade, foreign investment, joint ventures, academic exchange, industrial competition, and, in some cases, allegations of espionage or intellectual-property theft.

At the same time, espionage is hardly unique to China. The US has a long and well-documented history of conducting intelligence and espionage operations around the world through the CIA, NSA, and other agencies. So rather than reducing the history of U.S.–China technological competition to the claim that “China stole American technology,” it is worth looking at the much more complicated ways technology, knowledge, and industrial capabilities have moved between countries.

comments.name: Peter Prahar
comments.body:
The Editorial Board presents USDA's retreat on dairy sustainability as the end of a Biden-era "heist." The history says otherwise.

The Dairy Checkoff is not a fund Washington spends as it pleases. Under the Dairy Production Stabilization Act of 1983, farmer assessments go to boards run by dairy producers, chiefly through Dairy Management Inc. USDA's job is oversight. The sustainability programs now marked for termination were industry decisions made by farmers' own representatives.

Nor are they Biden inventions. The U.S. Dairy Net Zero Initiative was launched in 2020, during President Trump's first term, by the industry's Innovation Center for U.S. Dairy. Its logic was commercial, not ideological. Big buyers such as Nestlé and Starbucks demand emissions data and reductions from their suppliers, and export customers increasingly expect the same. Methane digesters and feed-efficiency research also let farmers earn revenue from renewable natural gas and cut input costs. That is demand-building by another name.

As for the  study asking whether removing dairy cows would help the climate, it cuts the other way. Its answer, published in the Journal of Dairy Science, was that eliminating dairy cows would trim U.S. greenhouse emissions by less than 1 percent while opening serious gaps in American nutrition. Commissioning rigorous analysis inoculates the industry against activist claims; shutting it down leaves dairy defenseless against external critics armed with their own bias.

You might assume that you’d praise Dateline as catching child predators but when you really go back and look at the facts of how they catfished and entrapped people, it felt very wrong (perhaps should be illegal) and unethical. Since the show used a vacant house, and the men who were arrested showed up there expecting to meet someone they believed to be a child, I’m having a hard time manifesting any  outrage. 

There isn’t a TV show or movie or influencer or DIYer posting videos online that doesn’t want publicity. Or a journalist, for that matter, so it’s hardly reasonable to expect otherwise. comments.name: Vanessa Friedman
comments.body:
I have spent a lot of my career focusing on what people in the public eye are wearing, and how that affects popular perception. Readers often ask me why I bother to write about this supposedly "fluffy" subject, especially when it comes to someone like Mark Zuckerberg, who wields an enormous amount of power in ways that are often seen as negative. 

My feeling is that the way someone constructs their image tells us a huge amount about how they want to be perceived -- how they are trying to manipulate our opinions -- and that is valuable information, perhaps most of all when they wield great power. For a more in-depth explanation of my approach to this, you can read our Q&A on the subject here*.

(*https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/insider/mark-zuckerberg-fashion-style.html)

comments.body:
“Aut Zuck aut nihil” is not a random phrase, but a reference to “Aut Caesar aut nihil,” meaning “Either Caesar or nothing,” a man seeking absolute power. If I recall my Latin, “aut…aut” is either/ or.

comments.body: Am I the only one who doesn't mind busy work? I find it somehow soothing - sometimes I get into an odd state of flow writing a document, analyzing an excel spreadsheet, et al. To the author's point, the minutiae of otherwise quotidian tasks belie a bevy of growth opportunities.

comments.name: Steve M
comments.body:
Yeah no kidding. 

Studies in colleges have found this out.  Students using AI can create great homework assignments but when they get to a test, or have to explain their reasoning without the aid of AI, they have no clue what they are doing.  They aren't putting in the thinking man hours required to build the basic skills required to pile on my complex thought and reasoning.  An athlete can't compete in a running marathon if the only miles they put in were on a bike.

And it's easy to say that doesn't matter and it's simply a new frontier...until you consider the surgeon example. Do you want surgery from a surgeon who has multiple times less experience than their forebears? That seems to be the world we're living in right now.

comments.name: George Walker
comments.body:
Thank you, Ms. Pohle, for your thought-provoking analysis. 

There may well be better ways to acquire “experience-based judgment” “than by getting in the reps,” which is how I and others of my generation acquired that initial foundational experience. And I’m all in favor of better ways to do things.

But I’ve also learned to be a little wary of “new and improved.”  And it begins with “improved” for whom, as well as what is lost? (Think T.S. Eliot’s The Rock: “Where is the knowledge we have lost in information?”)

I’m sure they’ll find a way to work it out. But at what cost to the “junior staff”?

You need to know how and what questions to ask to get meaningful answers. This is something akin to letting first graders use calculators for addition and subtraction. Quick answers, but no idea why!

comments.name: Steve W-T
comments.body:
We all want reliable electricity.  Solar helps but needs to be supplemented during darker seasons and at night.  Less light, less power production.  

We have solar panels which over a year provide most of our power needs.   However our utility, a hydroelectric system, fills in the gap when our solar is insufficient.  The utility even credits us power when we generate more than we need.

This benefits both sides.  The utility gets to store more water ready to be used to generate electricity later, to meet future electricity demands and maintain reliable service throughout the year.

comments.name: Otag
comments.body: Oberlin, Ohio, was able to restore power within hours during the 2003 blackout that affected Ohio to NY and Ontario because it has its own municipal power plant, allowing it to disconnect from the larger grid and restart its local generation. In contrast, many other areas experienced prolonged outages lasting up to four days. Smaller is better.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: I am curious about why this topic of micro-grids appears to be covered as a exciting new idea. I have seen stories here discussing this topics for a couple of years. Real estate developers looking to build a 500 house development with its own micro grip and a solar primary power source. Don't get me wrong. I think this idea needs to get covered any way we can to get it more readily accepted. But it ain't "wildly new from the forests of Sweden."

comments.name: Anon
comments.body: The organizations that I have been working with said this in the 1970s.

comments.name: Sunny
comments.body: Is smaller better? Consider the ancient survivors of the animal kingdom. Among those who have actually survived apocalyptic conditions are mosquitos, cockroaches, and our life-saving heroes, horseshoe crabs.

comments.name: Chad Borman
comments.body: Meanwhile, in the United States, we show almost know urgency to modernize our own electricidal grid.  We'll just continue with the same old technology until a catastrophe changes our minds.

comments.name: Ashley Dawson
comments.body: The technology may be new but the idea of energy networks linking microgrids in a resilient web is not. Amory and Hunter Lovins published their book "Brittle Power" in 1982 warning about the fragility of the US's centralized, top-down, for-profit electric utility system. What a pity it's taken so long for their ideas to find a champion.

comments.name: Luke
comments.body:
Bishop Sheen was one of the first televangelists and a Catholic rock star. My friends would bring their Kodak Instamatic cameras to church trying to get a photo with him. Like most saints, he was human and not infallible. He came out against the Vietnam War in 1967 and tried to donate a parish building to the Housing Urban Development program to benefit the black community. 
He was exonerated from placing a priest accused of sexual misconduct in Rochester because it happened before his time as bishop. 
As a recovering Catholic who grew up attending parochial school, it is difficult for me to believe he did not know of other priests who abused parishioners emotionally and physically. Instead of contacting the authorities they were dealt with internally and moved to other parishes or confined to an office. 
The church still tries to raise up those to sainthood as holier than thou. Saints capable of great works, moral superiority, and miraculously blessed. I believe in what Walt Whitman wrote as closer to the truth. "We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars." Love thy neighbor is still a very difficult path to follow for saints as well as sinners.

comments.name: B. Mc Cauley

As a lapsed catholic looking for faith/ belief in something in this distressed world it would be so nice to have the belief of a child.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: I always thought that a candidate for sainthood had to have carried out, been subject to, or involved in a miracle during their lifetime. The idea that someone prayed to him and the prayer bore out a miraculous outcome, is new to me.

comments.name: Ray Wood
comments.body: My father never went to church. But whenever Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen was on, my father tuned in with rapt attention, puctuated with laughter at the bishop's humor.

The sisters would ask us at school on Monday morning who watched Bishop Sheen. More judgment and intimidation. He had a charismatic aura for sure. In retrospect, wizard-like.

They told me that, unfortunately, he could not because the rules said "No Americans".  Seemed unfair to me, but ... hey ... I was just a kid. Anyway, now I'm a non-theist.  But Bishop Sheen holds a special place of reverence in my memory and my heart.  He was a clear thinker, a great speaker, and made excellent use of that blackboard!

comments.body: "Conversions are surging"? Pew's latest landscape study finds that for every American who converts to Catholicism, 8.4 raised in the faith have left, and the Catholic share of U.S. adults fell from 24 percent in 2007 to 19 percent, while the "42,000 conversions" the Times repeats is admittedly just what Sheen "was said to be responsible for." comments.name: Alex Alfaro
comments.body: And I must admit that I do keep falling in love with celebrity animals due to their cuteness and entertainment value. I guess my favorite one would be Punch, the baby monkey with a stuffed animal, as the story of how he ended up being so lonely made me feel sorry for him. I find Jimothy extremely amusing thanks to his unusual appearance and the popularity that he gained on the internet. As the author of the article, Aimee Frazier, states, “Jimothy ‘pulls us out of ourselves,’” which demonstrates the ability of animals to help people forget about their routine. I think that celebrity animals help unite people as everybody can watch and laugh at them.

comments.name: Josafat Maaz
comments.body: Personally I  have never liked looked deeper into celebrity animals but there is one animal  that I  like and his name is Punch the monkey. What made me like him was his story, thinking a plushie was his mother , and  him getting bullied by other monkeys but at the end being able to make friends. This is also accompanied by how cute he looks his , this was able to attract millions of fans around the world but punch the monkey shows people that even though they could or are being left out they will find a friend that will be there for them just like punch

comments.name: Sam
comments.body: I absolutely do keep falling in love with celebrity animals. They’re adorable, for one, and they also always have such sweet and specific names and stories, like the Halls being “blessed by a Jimothy.” Something about animals with certain tendencies, like carrying a stuffed animal or being smaller than normal, makes them infinitely more attractive than normal animals to me. Beyond that, I believe that plays into them going so viral. Humans have seen baby animals before, and although they’re cute they aren’t super exciting. When you bring another element into an already cute animal that makes them even more cute, people can’t handle it. A normal small animal, or a large animal with a unique trait like this, wouldn’t work; it has to be both.

comments.name: Vihaan Modi
comments.body: I do keep falling in love with celebrity animals because they are so cute and whenever something goes viral, I instantly build an interest in them. My favorite celebrity animal would have to be Jimothy because of the way he walks, his shape, and the fact that he is an adorable raccoon. All of these celebrity animals are becoming popular because of their convenience to humour on social media and throughout this generation. Animals that go viral are usually because they are adorable, they are a unique species, or maybe someone just made a funny joke. Punch is also my favorite celebrity animal because of its cute little plushie. Overall, celebrity animals are and always will be popular because they are cool and funny which gives them a lot of attention.

comments.name: Lily
comments.body: I fall in love with celebrity animals all the time! Although I love all animals, I have a special place in my heart for Punch-the orphaned monkey who bonded with his stuffed animal. Personally, I think the latest public appeal towards Jimothy is not only cute, but also necessary. Obviously, he is an adorable raccoon who has captured the hearts of millions of people across the globe, but, beyond that, it gives people a common source of joy. Even in the article, they talk about how Jimothy inspired a mural, a charity auction, and even cryptocurrency! In this current world, everyone seems to be disagreeing with everyone else, but Jimothy, is a weird, somewhat cute way, brings us all together. I think animals like Moo Deng, Punch, Chonkers, and Jimothy have all become so popular on social media because of they are adorable, but also just a little bit different than what someone might stereotypically think that animal should look or act like. Although there aren’t really any “official” animals that have lore in my town, there is a singular black squirrel that people get excited when they see.

comments.name: Pavel
comments.body: I love these celebrity animals, although I haven’t been keeping up with the latest ones nor have I been actively looking online for these animals. When they do occasionally get on my feed, I feel the “something special is happening here”. It’s always refreshing when people online decide to “adopt” an animal when the internet, or even the world, can feel chaotic. These animals seem to be recognized for their unique story or circumstance and, to me, they look like they know that they are famous. The only celebrity animal I know well from stories, also my favorite, is Punch, his story reminds me that better days are ahead of bad ones and that there are always people that can help you get through your struggles. Although “Animal celebrities” can be trends that people forget over time, I will remember what these animals mean to me and give thanks to those who care about these animals.

comments.name: Lizeth
comments.body: I think that since everyone is connecting over something so positive like these celebrity animals is comforting in a time where everything feels so divided. I know I for one have been very intrigued with these celebrity animals and my personal favorite has been Jimothy because I love raccoons so much and I was so happy to find others wanted to discuss them. Punch and Moo Deng are so cute and my feed was full of them, but I noticed something better when I'd look into the comments; People connected over their love for them! The rise in celebrity animals creates a positive space in places you wouldn't expect. I love these animals!

comments.name: Melody
comments.body: My algorithm does not typically bring celebrity animals to my attention, but whenever I do see them, I find them cute and entertaining. They’re usually small and cute, so oftentimes I would get cuteness aggression just from looking at them. I do not follow news of them extensively but welcome it if it is recommended to me. Recently, I have developed an infatuation with seals. Their overall behavior and faces are so adorable, so I understand where celebrity animal lovers are coming from. Of all the celebrity animals, I have to say Moo Deng is one of my favorites. Oftentimes, animals like her appear out of nowhere when people find a lovable animal somewhere, “[endow] it with a name, personality and opinions and [take] it in like an orphan,” making them become a “bona fide world celebrity” (Streeter, as cited in Engle). The same can be said for Moo Deng, as she suddenly became an internet superstar overnight. It can mainly be attributed to her cute stature and behavior, since people easily develop love and sympathy for creatures that look cute. Another one of my top favorites is Mei Mei, a cat in China that has become a tourist attraction. Beyond that, cute creatures taking over the internet is also a welcome distraction from the more depressing, stressful issues going on around the world. They provide a nice break in the algorithm, making people easily adore them. Overall, celebrity animals can be a great inclusion into everyone’s lives.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Time to talk about the Romans.  

And I'm thinking of Horace.  Who (in one of his satires) talks about a man whose clothing--shall we say?  

--is far from elegant.  The guy's a sloppy dresser.  His shoes don't fit. The toga looks as if he flung it on any which way.  

BUT--

--that same guy is possessed of a first rate mind.  He's sharp as a tack.  And in addition to that--

--he's a faithful friend and a patriotic Roman.  

I guess the clothes didn't much matter. 

Which brings us to Mr. Zuckerberg--

--and a million eyes busy scrutinizing his clothes.  

And I would ask:  why doesn't the stuff he actually DOES--

--and the stuff he actually SAYS--

--and the USE to which he puts those billions of smackers--

--matter more than whatever he happens to be wearing?  Such studiously casual clothing too!

--but that's the way billionaires dress nowadays.  

And hey!  I wouldn't presume to judge these guys--

comments.name: Guillaume
comments.body:
I understand the argument: clothes communicate, powerful people construct images, and examining that construction can reveal how they want us to see them.

Fair enough.

But recognizing the packaging is not the same as interrogating what is being packaged. In Zuckerberg’s case, the interesting question surely cannot stop at the hoodie, the chain, the shorts, or the rebrand. These are professionally managed signals from an extraordinarily powerful figure whose company has faced profound questions about manipulation, harm, responsibility, and accountability.

That context is precisely what makes the intense attention to his image feel so strangely myopic. If the clothes are meant to shape perception, then the journalism should do more than decode the strategy. It should resist being absorbed into it.

Otherwise, however perceptive the fashion analysis may be, we are still spending an extraordinary amount of cultural attention examining the packaging of someone who already has virtually unlimited means to package himself.

Please consider that your article didn't succeed at that worthy aim. If you read the comment section, you'll see that your point didn't come through for many readers. The paper also found it necessary to publish this supplemental article explaining and justifying itself, which it wouldn't need to do if the first article had made its own case successfully. I'd love to see more articles like this, but please try a different approach next time. My own suggestion would be to offer more answers to the provocative questions that justify writing the profile in the first place.

"Action films" can have very different thematics and styles. In the most 'pure' examples of the genre, the plot is window dressing for displays of physical and/or cinematic virtuosity. Like dance, it's mainly about appreciating choreography. OTOH are films with lots of action, but in the service of a more thematic driven story. Serious drama, if you will, which has never been simplistic happy ending territory. You don't paste a happy ending on Bridge Over the River Kwai, or Planet of the Apes for that matter. Maybe the two best action films of the 80s exemplify the two poles. Die Hard follows near-perfect execution of cinematic effects to an unambiguous happy ending. Has there ever been a more bittersweet ending than The Road Warrior, with the reveal of the feral kid's saved future, while Max is left alone to live only in memory? 

My point I guess is just that bittersweet isn't anything new, but just people trying to make good films, and examples of that go way back.

I have to go along with the other commenters here who, for one reason or another, don't bother with the NYFF.  For one thing, it costs a lot, and for another it's a struggle to get tickets and go there (especially from LA where I live).

And for another, what are good movies?  Distinctive ideas carried out in a supple way that provides intellectual and emotional truth. Despite the PR ballyhoo off of 70mm or IMAX, these technical issues don't, to my view, improve what good movies are.  Nor does seeing a good movie right "out of the gate" matter much when you've seen thousands as I, and other commenters here, have.

Besides, if you've set up streaming with a good monitor, high quality throughput, and multi-speaker sound nothing beats my wife and me sitting in the most comfortable chairs in the world (from Norway), with hot-to-trot instead of lukewarm popcorn, watching a movie.  What low cost and freedom!  If it's a great film, it's no greater in a theater at a somewhat earlier date.  If it's a fair film, we can feel free to comment upon it as it goes along.  If it's a bad film, we can turn it off as soon as our popcorn is done and switch easily to something else (such as sports).  And if it's a really bad film, we can ridicule every scene with a flow of bon mots that crack both of us up.

So, we will wait a bit for the new Pawlikowski or Lee Chang-dong.  Great directors are hard to find and we will be happy as heck to cherish the latest from these in our living/screening room.

comments.name: Damien S.
comments.body:
An a digital anthropologist, I like to remind my students the value and meaning of AI, like any technology--fire, a knife, nuclear energy--is determined socially: We decide what it is best used for, when it is appropriate, what guidelines should exist to keep us all safe, etc. Humans are of course sometimes good at this and sometimes bad--but it isn't something inherent to the technology itself that "causes" bad human behavior or disrupts healthy human relationships. 

AI can be used in ways to strengthen and enhance face-to-face human relationship, and in many instances is already being used (as are social media) in ways that keep us all more socially supported and interconnected. (See my substack post on this: https://damienstankiewicz.substack.com/p/calder-shows-us-how-an-ai-companion?r=1a4thq). The problem with Turkle and other outspoken AI critics is that they argue, often in black and white "AI-is-evil" terms, that the technology cannot ever contribute to, rather than detract from, human relationships. 
That's what we call "techno-determinism," and it's just not how technology works: it's social context that determines how and why tools are useful, not the other way around. Which is why we need more conversation on (and regulation of) these tools and what we want from them, rather than merely vilifying them.

comments.name: Aubree Kohler
comments.body:
I am in love with a work of fiction that connects humanity at such an animalistic, visceral level. Regardless of your personal opinions towards David or his choices, Cline guides the reader through the raw emotions that make us... human! I would hate David in real life, but aren’t we all just kids inside? Don’t we all have things that stick with us, that we wish had gone differently?
This stream-of-consciousness stylization is *chef’s kiss*. Cline took risks with this, making a decision to honor the emotional impacts of the work rather than stylize it into something more attractive, or “easy,” for readers. I can understand that this style is not everyone’s cup of tea (can’t relate). Choosing another method of telling David’s story would be to limit the reader’s ability to travel into his mind. To crawl into the mind of so many of our loved ones, as terrifying as that may be.
My favorite aspect of this novel is the simple fact that David is an unlikeable man. It brings so much depth to these ideas: that “bad” people, or just people we don’t agree with, have regrets, too. We all live, and we all die. Isn’t it refreshing to feel raw empathy and a connection to a character we might hate in real life?
“So couldn’t he have another chance? Now that he knew to look out for it?”
Don’t we all wish for another chance? To do the right thing, to live in the moment? It’s hard to describe that feeling, of knowing you messed up.
My next read would be "The Correspondent" :)
